description: We are a team of six members from diverse backgrounds, including software development, business administration, electromechanical engineering, and design. We combine technical, creative, and strategic skills to build innovative solutions.
summary:
Space Sentinel is a health-monitoring platform for astronauts on long missions, where medical help from Earth may be delayed or unavailable. Astronauts log sleep, mood, vital signs, symptoms and medications every day; a women’s health module tracks the menstrual cycle, and spacecraft data relevant to analyzing the possible causes of symptoms is integrated.

An AI agent generates the analyses and works offline, because it uses the data entered by the crew and NASA databases from past missions. Without assuming the body in space is the same as on Earth, it compares each data point daily with the reference the astronaut builds during the mission, with the ranges expected in flight, and with previous days, and it generates weekly, monthly and 90-day statistics. It also contrasts symptoms and experiences with documented experiences of earlier astronauts. It issues explainable alerts and preventive recommendations, without diagnoses, and always escalates serious symptoms.

It matters because on a Mars mission the astronaut will be the first observer of their own health, and sometimes the only one. Space Sentinel turns NASA’s accumulated experience into autonomy, prevention and informed decisions.
details:
What it does and how it works

Space Sentinel is a health-monitoring platform for astronauts on long missions, where immediate medical help and communication with Earth may be limited or nonexistent. Astronauts log sleep, mood, vital signs, symptoms and medications every day, and a women’s health module lets them track their menstrual cycle. The platform adds spacecraft data relevant to analyzing the possible causes of symptoms, such as the CO₂ level in the module, along with the mission day and type.

An AI agent generates the analyses and works without an Internet connection, because it relies on the data entered by the crew and on a knowledge base built from NASA reports and documented experiences of astronauts from past missions. Because the body changes in space, the system does not compare astronauts only with their health on Earth: it contrasts each data point with the reference the astronaut builds during the mission, with what is expected in flight, and with previous days. Beyond the daily analysis, it generates weekly, monthly and 90-day statistics to detect trends.

When it detects a change, it issues an explainable alert: what was observed, what it may relate to (always as a possibility, never as a diagnosis), what is worth verifying and what to do now. Preventive recommendations come in three levels: self-care, check, and escalate. Serious symptoms, such as chest pain, confusion or fainting, are always escalated through fixed rules. The system also considers the astronaut’s medications to warn about possible effects or combinations to review, without suggesting doses, and a missing data point or an offline sensor is shown as “insufficient data,” never as normal.

Benefits and expected impact

The project offers greater autonomy for the crew, relevant information at the moment it is needed, and early detection of changes before they become critical. Its expected impact is greatest on missions to the Moon or Mars, where evacuation may take weeks or may not be possible, and where the astronaut, or the crew medical officer, who is not always a physician, will be the first observer of their health. The architecture could also be adapted to other isolated environments with limited access to medical services.

Tools and technologies

The prototype was built with React and Vite, TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML and CSS on the frontend; SQLite and SQL for data, with a backend API connecting the data to the interface; and a Progressive Web App (PWA) that allows critical functions to be used offline. Development was done with Visual Studio Code, Node.js and npm, using GitHub for version control and Jira for planning. The team also used AI tools to support research, database design and development: ChatGPT, OpenCode, Codex and Claude.

Creativity

The project is creative because it interprets health according to the mission context rather than Earth-based values: it combines a personal in-flight reference, expected ranges, previous days and period-based statistics. Its AI agent works offline on crew and NASA databases, and its alerts separate the observed data, the change, the possible explanation and the action, so that a person without medical training can understand them.

In addition, in the tools and references we reviewed, we did not find continuous menstrual cycle tracking. For this reason, Space Sentinel includes a women’s health module that offers a more complete view of astronauts’ well-being and generates data that, with consent and privacy protection, could support future research.

Factors considered

The team took into account communication interruptions with Earth, the need for support when there is no link, ease of use for astronauts without medical training, the privacy of health data, adaptation to different mission types (ISS, Moon and Mars), and the inclusion of the needs of the entire crew. We also considered the reliability of data and sensors, and medical responsibility: the system does not diagnose, offers low-risk recommendations and escalates serious cases. The prototype uses simulated data, and its medical content requires validation by specialists before any real use.
